Lecture 20: Graphical Interpretation of the Derivative

Goal: Recover information about a function \( f \) from the graph of \( f' \).

1 Implementing the I/D and 1st Derivative Test

Problem 1.

Use the graph of \( f' \) shown in Figure 1 to determine the following about \( f \):

  1. Intervals of increase/decrease

    We need to determine the critical numbers of \(f\). I.e., when the derivative is \(0\) or undefined. When we are looking at the graph of \(f'\), critical numbers occur when the graph of \(f'\) touch the \(x\)-axis. Therefore, for this example, there is only one critical number (namely \(0\)).

    After that, we need to make a sign chart for \(f'\). I.e., determine when \(f'\) is positive and negative. Looking at the graph of \(f'\) we have:

    1. \(f'>0\) when the graph of \(f'\) is above the \(x\)-axis;
    2. \(f'< 0 \) when the graph of \(f'\) is below the \(x\)-axis.

    Using the sign chart in Figure 2, \(f\) is increasing on \((0,\infty)\) while \(f\) is decreasing on \((-\infty, 0)\).

  2. Positions of relative max/mins:

    3. By the 1st Derivative Test, \(f\) only has a relative minimum at \(x = 0\) (no relative maximums).

Crit. Nums \( \leftarrow f' = 0 \leftarrow \) when \( f \) touches the x-axis

Problem 2.

Use the graph of \( f' \) in Figure 3 to determine the following about \( f \):

  1. Intervals of increase/decrease

    The critical numbers of \(f\) are \(0\) and \(2\) (See Problem 1 for explanation why). Constructing the sign chart in a similar manner to Problem 1 we get Figure 4:

    Therefore, \(f\) is increasing on \( (-\infty, 0) \cup (2, \infty) \) while decreasing on \((0, 2)\).

  2. Positions of relative max/mins

    3. By the First Derivative Test, there is a relative maximum at \(x=0\) and a relative minimum at \(x = 2\).

2 Implementing the Concavity and 2nd Derivative Test

Problem 3.

Use the graph of \( f' \) shown in Figure 5 to determine the following about \( f \):

  1. When \( f \) is concave up VS. concave down

    2. We need to determine when \(f'' = 0\). Interpreting \(f''\) as \([f']'\), it is \(0\) when a line tangent \(f'\) has a slope of \(0\). One way to finding these is to find when \(f'\) has a relative maximum or minimum (since possible locations for Inflection Points are critical numbers of \(f'\)). Thus, the only possible location for an inflection point is \(x = 2\).

    We now need to determine when \(f''\) is positive or negative. To do so,

    1. \(f''(c) > 0\) at \(c\) when the slope of the tangent line at \(c\) is positive (i.e., the line "points upward");
    2. \(f''(c) < 0\) at \(c\) when the slope of the tangent line at \(c\) is negative (i.e., the line "points downward").

    Using this, we can make a sign chart of \(f''\) as in Figure 6 to conclude \(f\) is CD on \((-\infty, 2)\) and CU on \((2, \infty)\).

  2. Position of any inflection points

    Since concavity changes at \(2\), there is an IP at \( x = 2 \).

    Figure 7 depicts a crude drawing of \(f\) near \(x = 2\), emphasizing that concavity needs to change for a point to be an inflection point.

Problem 4.

Use the graph of \( f' \) in Figure 8 to determine the following about \( f \):

  1. When \( f \) is concave up VS. concave down

    2. The only possible locations for Inflection Points are \(-3\) and \(2\) (see Problem 3 for an explanation on how these are found).

    Using the sign chart in Figure 9, \(f\) is CU on \( (-\infty, -3) \cup (2, \infty)\) and CD on \( (-3, 2) \).

  2. Position of any inflection points

    Since concavity changes at both points, there are Inflection Points at \( x = -3\) and \(x = 2 \).

  3. Implement the 2nd Derivative Test

    The critical numbers are \( x = -5, 0, 3.5 \). We need to determine the sign of \(f''\) at these points. Thus, we draw tangent lines at these points are determine if the slope is positive or negative. By the Second Derivative Test,

    \( f''(-5) > 0 \) \( \Rightarrow \) \(f\) has a relative minimum at \( x = 5 \)

    \( f''(0) < 0 \) \( \Rightarrow \)\(f\) has a relative maximum at \(x = 0\)

    \( f''(3.5) > 0 \) \( \Rightarrow \) \(f\) has a relative minimum at \( x = 5 \)

    The 1st Derivative Test will most likely to easier to implement for these kinds of problems. However, I did want to demonstrate how the 2nd Derivative Test is done in this context.

3 Putting Everything Together

We now want to combine everything, so if we have the graph of \(f'\) we can discuss the basic shape of \(f\).

NOTE:

For the remainder of the problems, the graphs, sign charts, and final answers will be given. For an in-depth explanation, see Problems 1 and 3.

Problem 5

Use the graph of \( f' \) in Figure 10 to determine the following about \( f \):

  1. Intervals of Increase/Decrease:

    Critical numbers are \( x = 9, 18 \). Using the sign chart:

    \(f\) is decreasing on \((-\infty, 9)\) and increasing on \((9, \infty)\).

  2. When \( f \) is concave up VS concave down:

    Possible locations of Inflection Points are \(x = 12,18\). From the sign chart:

    We see \(f\) is CU on \((-\infty, 12) \cup (18,\infty)\) and CD on \((12,18)\).

  3. State the locations of any relative max/mins as well as inflection points:

    4. By the 1st Derivative Test, \(f\) does not have any relative maxima, but has a relative minimum at \(x = 9\). There are also Inflection Points at \(x=12,18\).

This gives us enough information to make a (very crude) sketch of \(f\).

Problem 6

Use the graph of \( f' \) in Figure 14 to determine the following about \( f \):

  1. Intervals of Increase/Decrease:

    The critical numbers are \(x = -1,1\). From the sign chart:

    We see \(f\) is always increasing. I.e., it is increasing on \( (-\infty, \infty) \)

  2. When \( f \) is concave up VS concave down

    The possible locations for the Inflection Points are \(x = -1, 0,1\). From the sign chart:

    One has \(f\) is CD on \((-\infty, -1) \cup (0,1)\) and CU on \((-1,0) \cup (1,\infty)\).

  3. State the locations of any relative max/mins as well as inflection points

    There are no relative extrema by the 1st Derivative Test. Moreover, all possible locations for Inflection Points are indeed inflection points. I.e., \(f\) has Inflection Points at \(x=-1,0,1\).

    4. We have enough information to make a (very crude) sketch of \(f\).

Problem 7

Use the graph of \( f' \) in Figure 18 to determine the following about \( f \):

  1. Intervals of Increase/Decrease

    The critical numbers are \( x = -2, 1 \). From the sign chart:

    We see \(f\) is increasing on \((-\infty, -2) \cup (1,\infty)\) and decreasing on \((-2,1)\).

  2. When \( f \) is concave up VS concave down:

    The only possible location for an Inflection Point is \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\). From the sign chart:

    \(f\) is CD on \((-\infty, -\frac{1}{2})\) and CU on \((-\frac{1}{2}, \infty)\).
  3. State the locations of any relative max/mins as well as inflection points

    By the 1st Derivative Test, \(f\) has a relative maximum at \(x = -2\) and a relative minimum at \(x =1\). Moreover, \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\) is indeed the location of an inflection point.

Problem 8

Use the graph of \( f' \) in Figure 21 to determine the following about \( f \):

  1. Intervals of Increase/Decrease:

    \(f\) only has one critical number, namely at \(x = 0\). From the sign chart:

    \(f\) is decreasing on \((-\infty, 0)\) and increasing on \((0, \infty)\).

  2. When \( f \) is concave up VS concave down:

    From the sign chart below, \(f\) is always CU.

  3. State the locations of any relative max/mins as well as inflection points

    \(f\) has a relative minimum at \(x = 0\) by the 1st Derivative Test. However, \(f\) does not have an inflection point at \(x = 0\) since concavity does not change.

  3. State the locations of any relative max/mins as well as inflection points

    Relative Minima at \( x = 0, 1 \)

    Relative Maxima at \( x = \frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{2} \)
